introduction: The guide gathers counsel on how a faith is to be shared: by deeds before words, by friendship, at one’s own table, in language suited to the hearer, with wisdom about time and place, and with patient care for those who have just begun. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. Much of the same counsel is found in older teachers. Confucius opens one corner of a subject and waits; Socrates calls himself a midwife; Plato’s good doctor talks with the patient; Paul feeds with milk, works at his trade, teaches from house to house and is gentle as a nurse; the Qur’an asks for wisdom, fair exhortation and the language of the hearer’s own people; Franklin learns to forbear contradiction. Other voices make the method harder. Thoreau would run from anyone coming to do him good, Mencius distrusts the wish to teach, Jesus condemns those who cross sea and land for one proselyte and yet says to preach from the housetops, Emerson wants hard words, and Vivekananda asks whether anyone needs to change religion at all. They are set where the guide’s own counsel of tact and reserve could be mistaken for something less honest.
questions: The guide says the best way to teach is by deeds. What in Chaucer's parson, Whitman's presence and Aristotle's account of character explains why?
Thoreau would run from a person who came to do him good. What would make a friendship offered by a teacher trustworthy to the one befriended?
Several readings ask the teacher to speak according to the hearer's capacity, and Paul asks whether he is merely pleasing men. How do you tell adaptation from flattery or concealment?
Jesus says both not to cast pearls before swine and to preach from the housetops. What decides, in a given place and time, which saying applies?
Socrates calls teaching midwifery and Pascal says people are best persuaded by reasons they find themselves. What would a conversation guided by those two ideas sound like?
The guide insists that new believers must not be left to themselves. What does Peter's charge to feed the lambs add to a plan for systematic instruction?

outside.why: Confucius describes the superior man in the same order: he acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
Chaucer's parson gave his sheep this example, that first he wrought and afterward he taught.
James asks what it profits to tell the naked and hungry to depart in peace and be warmed and filled, while giving them nothing.
Franklin made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction of the sentiments of others, and all positive assertion of his own.
Emerson would have a person speak what he thinks now in hard words, though it contradict everything said before. What is lost, and what gained, by the gentler way described here?
Whitman says of himself and his kind that they do not convince by arguments, similes or rhymes, but by their presence.
Plato's free doctor carries his inquiries far back, goes into the nature of the disorder, and enters into discourse with the patient.
At the well Jesus begins by asking a woman of Samaria for a drink, and only then speaks to her of living water.
Paul says the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle to all, apt to teach, patient, instructing in meekness.
Mencius says that the evil of men is that they like to be teachers of others. How does one share a truth without that liking creeping in?
The Dhammapada has each man direct himself first to what is proper, and only then teach others.
Paul says he came in weakness and fear, and that his preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom.
Aristotle holds that persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character, since we believe good men more fully and more readily.
Philip does not argue with Nathanael's doubt that any good thing can come out of Nazareth; he says only, come and see.
Aristotle says one cannot be a friend to many people in the perfect sense. Is a friendship begun in order to teach a friendship in his sense, and how would the friend know?
Thoreau says that if he knew a man was coming to his house with the conscious design of doing him good, he would run for his life. What must be true of a teacher for that fear to be groundless?
In Jesus's parable the shepherd leaves the ninety and nine to go after the one that is lost, until he finds it.
Hebrews asks its readers not to forget to entertain strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares.
Bacon rates discretion above eloquence: to speak agreeably to the person we deal with is more than to speak in good words or good order.
John tells of Joseph of Arimathaea, a disciple but secretly, out of fear, who came forward to ask for the body of Jesus.
Confucius does not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge, and presents one corner of a subject at a time.
The Qur'an says that no messenger was ever sent save with the language of his folk, that he might make the message clear to them.
Paul uses the same figure of his own teaching: I have fed you with milk and not with meat, for you were not able to bear it.
Mark says that Jesus spoke the word to the people in parables, as they were able to hear it.
Confucius explains why he urged one pupil forward and kept another back: one was retiring and slow, the other had more than his share of energy.
Jesus warns against casting pearls where they will be trampled under foot, and the giver turned upon.
Jesus tells his disciples to speak in the light what they heard in darkness, and to preach it upon the housetops. When does reserve become a failure to say what one has been given?
Jesus tells his own disciples that he has many things yet to say which they cannot bear now.
Paul describes himself among new believers as gentle, even as a nurse cherishes her children.
Paul asks whether he seeks to please men, and says that if he did he would not be the servant of Christ. Where does fitting one's words to the hearer end and pleasing the hearer begin?
Paul would rather speak five words with his understanding, so as to teach others, than ten thousand in an unknown tongue.
Aristotle observes that anyone can give or grow angry, but to do it to the right person, at the right time and in the right way is not easy.
The Qur'an gives the same pair: call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason in the better way.
Zechariah hears how the work is to be done: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

Locke gives every man a commission to admonish, exhort and convince by reasoning, and reserves compulsion to the magistrate. Why should persuasion be the only instrument a teacher of religion may use?
Paul quotes a call that works like the morning breeze: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.
Proverbs observes that a soft answer turns away wrath, while grievous words stir up anger.
Matthew applies the prophet's words to Jesus: he shall not strive nor cry, and a bruised reed shall he not break.

The first Christian teachers were accused of having turned the world upside down and of acting contrary to Caesar's decrees. Can a new message be taught without raising a clamour, and should it always try to?
A saying of Muhammad asks that his teachings be conveyed to the people even if it were a single sentence.
Paul's charge to Timothy has the same urgency: preach the word, be instant in season and out of season.
Peter asks believers to be ready always to give an answer to everyone who asks a reason of the hope that is in them.
Philip hears a traveller reading the prophet Isaiah, and begins with a question about what he is already reading.
Socrates calls his art midwifery: he attends men and looks after their souls when they are in labour. Is teaching a matter of supplying proofs, or of helping another bring a conviction to birth?
Paul reminds the elders that he kept back nothing profitable, and taught them publicly and from house to house.
Apollos, an eloquent man and mighty in the scriptures, is taken aside by Aquila and Priscilla and shown the way of God more perfectly.
A letter of Paul says that women should keep silence in the churches. What changes when women are named among the chief teachers of a faith?
Plato's Socrates complains that written words, like the creations of a painter, preserve a solemn silence when asked a question. What can a living teacher do that the best book cannot?
Paul tells Timothy to commit what he has heard to faithful men who shall be able to teach others also.
Moses asks that the words be taught diligently to the children, at home and by the way, at lying down and at rising up.
In Revelation the one who knocks at the door asks to come in and sup with whoever opens.

Jesus tells a host not to invite the friends and rich neighbours who can repay him, but the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind. Who is usually invited to the table where a faith is shared, and who is left out?
Jesus says that he must work while it is day, for the night comes when no man can work.
Hebrews asks believers not to forsake assembling together, but to consider and exhort one another.
In Proverbs wisdom cries without and utters her voice in the streets. Why might a faith forbid, in a given time and place, what wisdom herself is pictured doing?
Confucius counts two errors: not to speak to a man who may be spoken with, and to speak to one who may not.
The psalmist's prayer before speaking is brief: O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall show forth thy praise.
Moses prays in the Qur'an that his mind be relieved, his task eased and a knot loosed from his tongue, so that they may understand.
Jesus sends his disciples to heal the sick and adds: freely ye have received, freely give.
Jesus points to the image and superscription on the coin, and separates what is to be rendered to Caesar from what is to be rendered to God.
Jesus sends his travelling teachers out lightly: no purse, no scrip, no shoes, and peace spoken to each house.
Jesus rebukes those who compass sea and land to make one proselyte and leave him worse than themselves. What separates the travelling asked for here from the travelling he condemns?
Paul and Barnabas return through the cities where they had taught, confirming the souls of the disciples.
Paul asks for a circumspect walk that redeems the time, because the days are evil.
At Corinth Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla and works at their common craft, for by occupation they were tentmakers.
Paul calls himself a wise masterbuilder who has laid the foundation, on which another builds.
In Jesus's parable the sower's seed falls by the way side and on good ground alike, and the good ground brings forth fruit.
Paul divides the labour: I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
The Preacher says to sow in the morning and not withhold the hand in the evening, since no one knows which will prosper.
Jesus quotes the saying that one sows and another reaps. Can a teacher be content never to see the harvest, and what does that do to the manner of sowing?
Paul uses the image of fragrance too: the savour of the knowledge of God made manifest in every place.
Isaiah's invitation is a cup-bearer's cry: come to the waters, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Jeremiah tried to keep silent, but the word was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones.
At Pentecost the image is literal: cloven tongues like as of fire, and speech as the Spirit gave utterance.
The council marvels at Peter and John, perceiving that they were unlearned and ignorant men who had been with Jesus.
Paul reminds his church that not many wise, mighty or noble were called, and that God chose the foolish things to confound the wise.
Pope warns that a little learning is a dangerous thing and that shallow draughts intoxicate the brain. If the unlearned taught the world, what did they have that his shallow drinker lacks?
Paul says the treasure is kept in earthen vessels so that the excellency of the power may be of God and not of us.
Paul became as weak to the weak, and was made all things to all men, that he might save some. Is approaching people through what they already hold a form of respect, or of concealment?
The two at Emmaus ask one another whether their heart did not burn within them while he talked with them by the way.
Paul, speaking to one king, hears him say 'almost thou persuadest me', and wishes all who hear were as he is.
Jesus calls his followers the light of the world and says that a city set on a hill cannot be hid.
Moses pleads that he is not eloquent, but slow of speech and of a slow tongue.
Paul tells those with gifts differing to use the one each has been given, whether prophecy or ministry.
Portia says it is a good divine that follows his own instructions, and that she could easier teach twenty than be one of the twenty. Why does so much depend on the teacher's own person?
Pascal observes that people are generally better persuaded by the reasons they have themselves discovered than by those of others.
Pope's rule for the critic serves the teacher: men must be taught as if you taught them not.
Vivekananda holds that the Christian is not to become a Hindu or a Buddhist, nor they Christians, but each to assimilate the spirit of the others. What does that ask of anyone who teaches a faith?
Ashoka's edict says that whoever praises his own religion while condemning others only harms his own, and that contact between religions is good.
The Qur'an tells its people not to argue with the People of the Scripture unless in a way that is better.
Paul calls his converts little children for whom he travails in birth again until Christ be formed in them.
Paul tells the Corinthians that they may have ten thousand instructors and yet not many fathers.
Peter is asked whether he loves, and is told to feed the lambs and the sheep. Why is the care of those already gathered tied to love and not to skill?
Paul recalls how he exhorted, comforted and charged every one of his converts, as a father does his children.
Jesus sends seventy ahead of him two by two and says that the harvest is great but the labourers are few.
Hebrews reproaches those who ought by now to be teachers and still have need of milk and not of strong meat.
Paul describes his own aim as warning every man and teaching every man in all wisdom.
Paul lists apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers as given for the perfecting of the saints.
Mill called a general State education a mere contrivance for moulding people to be exactly like one another. What keeps a systematic programme of religious instruction from the same danger?
The charge at the end of Matthew is to go and teach all nations, teaching them to observe all that was commanded.

peter-won-without-the-word.text: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives; While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear

acts-expounded-more-perfectly.text: And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus. This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John. And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly

acts-publickly-and-from-house-to-house.text: And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publicly, and from house to house

matthew-not-strive-nor-cry.text: He shall not strive, nor cry; neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory

acts-they-were-tentmakers.text: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth; And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them. And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers. And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks

corinthians-wise-masterbuilder.text: According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon

romans-gifts-differing.text: Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering: or he that teacheth, on teaching; Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness

john-feed-my-lambs.text: So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs. He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep

colossians-teaching-every-man.text: Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus

acts-confirming-the-souls.text: And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch, Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God. And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed

luke-call-the-poor-to-thy-feast.text: Then said he also to him that bade him, When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee. But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just

john-give-me-to-drink.text: There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink. (For his disciples were gone away unto the city to buy meat.) Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water

thessalonians-as-a-father-doth-his-child.text: As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children, That ye would walk worthy of God, who hath called you unto his kingdom and glory

aristotle-character-most-effective-persu.text: Persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character when the speech is so spoken as to make us think him credible. We believe good men more fully and more readily than others: this is true generally whatever the question is, and absolutely true where exact certainty is impossible and opinions are divided. This kind of persuasion, like the others, should be achieved by what the speaker says, not by what people think of his character before he begins to speak. It is not true, as some writers assume in their treatises on rhetoric, that the personal goodness revealed by the speaker contributes nothing to his power of persuasion; on the contrary, his character may almost be called the most effective means of persuasion he possesses
aristotle-character-most-effective-persu.author: Aristotle

pascal-reasons-they-have-themselves-disc.text: People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others
pascal-reasons-they-have-themselves-disc.author: Blaise Pascal

franklin-forbear-all-direct-contradictio.text: I made it a Rule to forbear all direct Contradiction to the Sentiments of others, and all positive Assertion of my own
franklin-forbear-all-direct-contradictio.author: Benjamin Franklin

proverbs-wisdom-crieth-in-the-streets.text: Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets: She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words
